title: How Play-Doh Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history and chemistry of Play-Doh. They open with banter about T-shirts and Chuck's childhood memories of Play-Doh paste. The history covers Joe McVicker's wallpaper-cleaning putty from Cincinnati, his sister-in-law's idea to make it a toy, the 1956 launch, Captain Kangaroo's promotion (Bob Keeshan), the Rainbow Crafts Company, Play-Doh Pete, and the Fun Factory extruder. They cover production figures and licensing, then the chemistry: wheat starch (amylose and amylopectin), gelatinization, retrogradation, lubricants (mineral oil), surfactants, salt as preservative, and colors. They discuss homemade recipes, 3D Play-Doh printers, banned Play-Doh ads, and a listener email about PG-13 movies and the single F-bomb rule.

segments.title: Opening banter and T-shirts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about their voices, new Stuff You Should Know T-shirts, and the contest designs. They say they will talk about Play-Doh.

segments.title: Childhood memories and Play-Doh perfume
segments.summary: Chuck jokes about eating Play-Doh paste as a kid. They mention a 2006 fiftieth-anniversary celebration and a Play-Doh-scented perfume.

segments.title: Origins: Joe McVicker and wallpaper cleaner
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Play-Doh started as a wallpaper cleaning putty made by Joe McVicker's family soap company, Cookson Products, in Cincinnati. Coal heating left soot on walls. Natural gas later hurt sales. McVicker's sister-in-law, a teacher, saw kids making ornaments from the putty and suggested turning it into a toy.

segments.title: Captain Kangaroo deal and early marketing
segments.summary: A non-toxic version with almond scent was made. McVicker donated cans to Cincinnati schools. Captain Kangaroo host Bob Keeshan was offered two percent of gross sales to mention the product on the show. He increased the mentions to three times a week. The company was named Rainbow Crafts, and the original four colors were red, blue, yellow, and white.

segments.title: Play-Doh Pete and packaging history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the packaging mascots: an elf designed by wildlife artist John Ruthven, then Play-Doh Pete, the kid in a smock and beret. In 2002 Pete got a baseball cap, and later the can became a character with arms.

segments.title: Cleanup, modeling, and the Fun Factory extruder
segments.summary: They discuss why Play-Doh dries out and is hard to make permanent, and cleanup tips for carpet, including avoiding warm water. They describe the Fun Factory extruder from General Electric engineers. Sales figures are given: about 950 million pounds and more than two billion cans since 1956, and roughly 100 million cans a year now.

segments.title: Licensing, fake food, and ingredients
segments.summary: Play-Doh has licensing deals, including Disney Princess sets, and past fake-food ads such as Pizza Hut pizzas. The hosts list the general ingredient categories: water, wheat starch, a retrogradation inhibitor, salt, lubricant, surfactant, preservative, hardener, humectant, fragrance, and color. The fragrance was almond at first, and Play-Doh has since admitted to vanilla.

segments.title: The chemistry of Play-Doh
segments.summary: Starch is made of amylose and amylopectin. Warm water gelatinizes starch into a gel. Excess amylose causes retrogradation, which makes the dough dry and brittle. Amylopectin is added to keep the dough pliable, which makes it sticky. Mineral oil is a lubricant. A surfactant holds the oil and water together. Salt was added and a chemist was brought in to adjust the salt level.

segments.title: Shelf life and making homemade Play-Doh
segments.summary: The hosts discuss shelf life and the Twinkies episode. They describe homemade recipes that use starch, water, and lubricant, and mention a cream of tartar recipe, a peanut butter variety, and glow-in-the-dark and glitter recipes. They suggest making it with kids as a chemistry lesson.

segments.title: Play-Doh 3D printers and banned ads
segments.summary: Two Play-Doh 3D printers are on the market, including one that plugs into an iPad. The hosts also discuss a Singapore series of banned, adult-themed Play-Doh ads that Hasbro denounced. They explain scam ads made by agencies to win awards.

segments.title: Listener mail: PG-13 F-bomb
segments.summary: A listener from Kauai writes about sneaking into R-rated movies as a kid and counting profanity. He says PG-13 films get one F-bomb. He cites Anchorman, Skyfall, Lincoln, Oblivion, and Edge of Tomorrow.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts mention ways to contact the show, including Twitter, Facebook, and email, and the website.
